\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

%% ¶1: Background + Context
AI agent systems produce heterogeneous execution traces spanning
prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects.
As deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of thousands of
calls, both developers and automated analysis agents need aggregate
views, including which categories of work consume the most tokens, where
failures concentrate, and how cost distributes across semantic task
families.

%% ¶2: Problem + example
However, no existing observability tool folds events across sessions
into an aggregate cost distribution. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, and OpenTelemetry
GenAI~\cite{otel} organize events into per-execution timelines and
span trees, enabling single-run debugging but not cross-session
aggregation. In a real development project, the system effect
\texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok} appears 2{,}903 times
across 325 sessions, yet no existing trace tool can disaggregate these
executions by the semantic intent that triggered them.

%% ¶3: Root cause
CPU profilers solved the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} fold millions of function-call samples
into a single chart where width represents cost. The key enabler is
\emph{deterministic} function names that merge identical call stacks.
Agent traces break this precondition because prompts are natural
language, and
two prompts expressing the same intent share no characters
(\S\ref{sec:background}).

%% ¶4: Existing solutions fail
Some existing tools take steps toward semantic grouping. Datadog LLM
Observability clusters user messages by
topic,\footnote{\url{https://docs.datadoghq.com/llm_observability/}}
and Laminar extracts structured signals from
traces.\footnote{\url{https://docs.lmnr.ai/signals/introduction}} Both characterize \emph{input distributions} (``30\% of users ask code
questions'') but not \emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks
consume 40\% of the token budget'').

%% ¶5: Key insight
We observe that agent observability requires \emph{semantic profiling},
meaning aggregate, cross-session cost attribution grouped by user
intent, as distinct from execution-structural groupings like sessions or
spans. The obstacle is the nondeterminism of natural-language identifiers.
Intent recognition can restore deterministic labels, making semantic
profiling tractable.

%% ¶6: This paper + numbers
This paper presents \toolname, a profiler that restores aggregate
flame-graph analysis for agent traces. The profiler is built on two
abstractions: an \emph{operation} (a uniform weighted record for any
agent activity) and an \emph{operation stack} (a field projection chosen
at query time). \toolname recovers the deterministic-label precondition through
\emph{intent recognition}, which maps free-form prompts to stable labels
using pluggable backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, or
unsupervised clustering). On 325 real sessions, semantic labels separate
90\% of system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public
datasets,
operation-stack profiling reduces inspection work by 90\% versus flat
summaries.

%% ¶7: Contributions
This paper makes three contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Insight: agent profiling reduces to two abstractions.}
  We show that fixed session/span hierarchies cannot fold by semantic
  category, and that combining uniform operation records with query-time
  stack projections closes this aggregation gap once intent recognition
  restores deterministic labels
  (\S\ref{sec:background}--\S\ref{sec:design}).
\item \textbf{System: \toolname.}
  We implement this model as a Rust CLI with pluggable intent
  recognition, four built-in views, and output formats (pprof, SVG,
  JSON) consumable by both developers and automated analysis agents
  (\S\ref{sec:impl}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation.}
  We show that semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight
  that unsemantic views merge (RQ1), that operation-stack profiling
  localizes hidden labeled problems with 90\% less work than flat
  summaries (RQ2), and that mapping-derived labels agree with
  ground-truth annotations on 7/9 public datasets (RQ3)
  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Background and Motivation}
\label{sec:background}

142	\subsection{How Existing Agent Trace Models Work}
143	
144	Current agent observability tools organize traces around fixed
145	hierarchies. OpenTelemetry represents an execution as a \emph{trace}
146	containing a tree of \emph{spans}, each with a name, duration, and
147	key-value attributes. LangSmith and Langfuse group spans into
148	\emph{sessions} and display them as timelines or waterfall charts.
149	Phoenix and OpenInference add GenAI-specific span types for LLM calls,
150	tool invocations, retrieval steps, and agent reasoning.
151	
152	These models share a structural property, namely that the session or
153	span tree is the skeleton of the data. Every event belongs to exactly one span, and
154	spans nest in a fixed parent-child hierarchy determined at execution
155	time. This design is effective for debugging because a developer can
156	locate a failing span, inspect its attributes, and trace its parent
157	chain to understand the execution context.
158	
159	\subsection{Why Fixed Hierarchies Cannot Profile}
160	
161	Profiling requires a fundamentally different operation, \emph{folding}
162	events across executions by semantic category so that width represents
163	aggregate cost. Fixed session/span hierarchies obstruct this in three
164	ways.
165	
166	First, sessions are boundaries, not categories. A single session may
167	contain review, debugging, and refactoring phases, and splitting by
168	session assigns all of them to the same bucket. Conversely, two sessions
169	performing the same task produce separate buckets that cannot be merged
170	without external logic. Second, span names describe mechanisms
171	(\texttt{LLMCall}, \texttt{ToolInvoke}, \texttt{ChatCompletion}), not
172	user intent (\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{test}). Grouping
173	by span name tells you how many LLM calls occurred, not which categories
174	of work consumed the budget. Third, these limitations compound in practice. A common system effect
175	like running a test suite may appear thousands of times across sessions,
176	but a flat process summary shows only a single counter with no way to
177	attribute executions to the semantic intent that triggered them. We
178	quantify this disaggregation in RQ1~(\S\ref{sec:eval}).
179	
180	\subsection{Why CPU Profiling Does Not Directly Apply}
181	
182	CPU profilers solve the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
183	A flame graph~\cite{flamegraphs} represents a profile as a set of
184	weighted \emph{samples}, each attached to a \emph{call stack} (an
185	ordered list of function frames). Identical stacks merge, and width
186	represents aggregate cost. The key enabler is that function names are
187	\emph{deterministic}. The same code path always produces the same
188	frames.
189	
190	Agent traces break this precondition. Prompts are natural language and
191	lack deterministic identifiers. Tool calls, GUI
192	actions, and process events are named heterogeneously across agent
193	families. Raw event names cannot serve as flame-graph frames.
194	
195	These observations yield three design requirements:
196	
197	\begin{description}
198	\item[R1: Uniform record type.]
199	  Agent traces mix prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions,
200	  process events, and benchmark labels. The profiler needs a single
201	  record type that can represent all of them without type-specific
202	  objects.
203	\item[R2: Query-time aggregation.]
204	  The same data must support multiple aggregation shapes (by task,
205	  phase, action, session, or dataset) without rebuilding the trace.
206	  Sessions and spans must be fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
207	\item[R3: Deterministic labels for folding.]
208	  Free-form prompts must be mapped to short, stable, repeatable labels
209	  before folding. This \emph{intent recognition} step has no analogue in
210	  CPU profiling, where function names are already deterministic.
211	\end{description}
212

\label{sec:background}

\subsection{How Existing Agent Trace Models Work}

Current agent observability tools organize traces around fixed
hierarchies. OpenTelemetry represents an execution as a \emph{trace}
containing a tree of \emph{spans}, each with a name, duration, and
key-value attributes. LangSmith and Langfuse group spans into
\emph{sessions} and display them as timelines or waterfall charts.
Phoenix and OpenInference add GenAI-specific span types for LLM calls,
tool invocations, retrieval steps, and agent reasoning.

These models share a structural property, namely that the session or
span tree is the skeleton of the data. Every event belongs to exactly one span, and
spans nest in a fixed parent-child hierarchy determined at execution
time. This design is effective for debugging because a developer can
locate a failing span, inspect its attributes, and trace its parent
chain to understand the execution context.

\subsection{Why Fixed Hierarchies Cannot Profile}

Profiling requires a fundamentally different operation, \emph{folding}
events across executions by semantic category so that width represents
aggregate cost. Fixed session/span hierarchies obstruct this in three
ways.

First, sessions are boundaries, not categories. A single session may
contain review, debugging, and refactoring phases, and splitting by
session assigns all of them to the same bucket. Conversely, two sessions
performing the same task produce separate buckets that cannot be merged
without external logic. Second, span names describe mechanisms
(\texttt{LLMCall}, \texttt{ToolInvoke}, \texttt{ChatCompletion}), not
user intent (\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{test}). Grouping
by span name tells you how many LLM calls occurred, not which categories
of work consumed the budget. Third, these limitations compound in practice. A common system effect
like running a test suite may appear thousands of times across sessions,
but a flat process summary shows only a single counter with no way to
attribute executions to the semantic intent that triggered them. We
quantify this disaggregation in RQ1~(\S\ref{sec:eval}).

\subsection{Why CPU Profiling Does Not Directly Apply}

CPU profilers solve the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
A flame graph~\cite{flamegraphs} represents a profile as a set of
weighted \emph{samples}, each attached to a \emph{call stack} (an
ordered list of function frames). Identical stacks merge, and width
represents aggregate cost. The key enabler is that function names are
\emph{deterministic}. The same code path always produces the same
frames.

Agent traces break this precondition. Prompts are natural language and
lack deterministic identifiers. Tool calls, GUI
actions, and process events are named heterogeneously across agent
families. Raw event names cannot serve as flame-graph frames.

These observations yield three design requirements:

\begin{description}
\item[R1: Uniform record type.]
  Agent traces mix prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions,
  process events, and benchmark labels. The profiler needs a single
  record type that can represent all of them without type-specific
  objects.
\item[R2: Query-time aggregation.]
  The same data must support multiple aggregation shapes (by task,
  phase, action, session, or dataset) without rebuilding the trace.
  Sessions and spans must be fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\item[R3: Deterministic labels for folding.]
  Free-form prompts must be mapped to short, stable, repeatable labels
  before folding. This \emph{intent recognition} step has no analogue in
  CPU profiling, where function names are already deterministic.
\end{description}

%% ===================================================================
\section{Design}

# Idea Quality Checklist for Systems Papers

What makes contributions, insights, and problem framing strong in OSDI/SOSP-tier papers.

---

## Section 1: Problem Framing

### What a good problem statement does
- Names a **concrete, painful consequence** of the status quo — not "challenges exist" but "tool X deletes your SSH keys"
- Identifies the **root cause** separately from symptoms — "the root cause is shared capability" not "tools sometimes misbehave"
- Is **multi-dimensional** when the problem is — security + safety + resource, not just one angle
- Makes the reader feel the problem before offering the solution

### Common problems
- **Single-dimension framing.** Only mentioning security when the system also helps with safety and efficiency. Reviewers ask "is this only useful against prompt injection?"
- **Symptom-only.** Listing what goes wrong without explaining WHY it goes wrong structurally
- **Straw-man gap.** Dismissing existing solutions too quickly without engaging with what they actually do
- **Scope creep.** Problem statement promises more than the paper delivers

### Tests
- Can you state the problem without mentioning your system? (If not, it's a solution looking for a problem)
- Does the root cause explain WHY the symptom occurs? (If it just restates the symptom, dig deeper)
- Would a reader who doesn't believe in prompt injection still care? (If not, the framing is too narrow)

---

## Round 1 — Problem Framing Review

### What works well

1. **Concrete consequence.** The cargo-test example (line 69: `process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok` appearing 2,903 times across 325 sessions with no way to disaggregate by intent) is excellent. It names a specific, quantified pain point before offering the solution.

2. **Root cause identified separately from symptoms.** ¶3 (lines 74–81) cleanly separates the structural root cause — agent prompts are natural language and lack deterministic identifiers — from the symptom (no cross-session aggregation). The CPU-profiler analogy makes the gap concrete: function names are deterministic, prompt names are not.

3. **Problem stated without the system.** Yes — the problem is fully articulable without mentioning AgentPProf: "No existing agent observability tool can fold events across sessions by semantic category because prompts lack the deterministic labels that flame-graph folding requires." Passes the solution-looking-for-a-problem test.

4. **Background section (§2) is well-structured.** The three-part argument (fixed hierarchies can't profile → CPU profiling doesn't directly apply → three requirements) is clean and each subsection does one job.

### Problems found

**1. Single-dimension framing — cost attribution dominates, crowding out other dimensions. (Important)**

The intro frames the problem almost entirely around cost/budget attribution: "which categories of work consume the most tokens" (line 58), "aggregate cost distribution" (line 64), "resource attribution" (line 90), "cost distributes across semantic task families" (line 59). Yet the evaluation (RQ2) also addresses failure localization, safety violations, redundant steps, and human-task boundaries — dimensions the intro barely mentions. Lines 58–60 list failures and cost but treat them as a list, not as independent pain dimensions that each independently motivate the system.

*Suggestion:* Expand ¶1 or ¶2 to give failure/safety/quality equal weight alongside cost. A second concrete example showing failure concentration ("unsafe operations cluster in navigation phases but no trace tool can show this") would make the problem genuinely multi-dimensional.

**2. ¶4 dismisses existing partial solutions too briefly — borderline straw-man. (Important)**

Lines 84–90 name Datadog and Laminar but dismiss them in two sentences with only the "input distributions vs. resource attribution" distinction. A reviewer who knows these tools may feel their capabilities are undersold. The distinction itself is valid, but the paragraph doesn't engage with *why* these tools stop at input distributions (is it architectural? deliberate scope choice?), making it feel like a drive-by dismissal.

*Suggestion:* Add one sentence explaining the structural reason these tools cannot do resource attribution (e.g., they cluster at the request level but don't propagate labels to downstream system effects). This turns the dismissal into an architectural argument.

**3. The abstract front-loads system mechanics before the reader feels the problem. (Minor)**

Lines 30–38 jump to "two abstractions" and "pluggable intent-recognition backends" before the reader has internalized why this matters. The abstract's problem statement (lines 23–29) is only 2.5 sentences. The intro does this much better (¶1–¶3 build the problem before ¶5–¶6 introduce the solution).

*Suggestion:* In the abstract, give one more sentence to the pain (e.g., the cargo-test disaggregation example compressed to one clause) before pivoting to the solution.
